label: paragraph_title
text: THOSE RENTS.

label: text
text: On every hand the evidence is accumulating in regard to the increase of rents in the Colony. There are two sides to every case, and it is a coincidence that the respective versions are set out in our correspondence "columns today."

label: text
text: The first, from a Kowloon resident, puts his plea for a Fair Rents Board very fairly and moderately. His arguments should strengthen the hands of the Kowloon Residents' Association, about 90 per cent. of whose membership is reported to favour the creation by the Government of a Fair Rents Board.

label: text
text:
It cannot be gainsaid that the landlords have been as badly hit as other people by the conditions prevailing during the past fifteen months. In some cases a certain increase in rent could not be grudged. That 15 per cent. permitted by the "Government—to which one of our correspondents to-day refers—was at least reasonable, even although the very natural and human tendency on the part of people who do not own their own houses is to resist all and every increase in rent. How much further landlords can go beyond that 15 per cent. without being actually oppressive is not a question for us to discuss. Each case can only be taken on its merits. And that, again, can only be decided fairly and equitably by a Fair Rents Board.
In regard to the views of the owner, also published to-day, he

label: text
text: These increases in rents were bound to follow the withdrawal of the protection to tenants afforded by the Rents Ordinance. In many cases, indeed, during the last fifteen months, landlords, in letting houses to new tenants, have carefully pointed out that such rents would hold good only for the duration of the strike and boycott, and that an increase must be expected afterward. In taking away the Rents Ordinance the authorities have taken away every prop of protection that many tenants had. There is now nothing for them to fall back on, and the only choice before them is to pay one, two, or half a dozen increases in rent—or clear out to other premises where they may possibly fare worse.

label: text
text: kind of contention altogether. He condemns the “principal tenant,” and gives a flagrant case of what is nothing more and nothing less than “squeeze.” In all the arguments submitted during the past eighteen months in favour of the retention of the Rents Ordinance on the Statute-book we have always held that many of the evils of high rents must be laid at the door of “principal tenants.” On one occasion we went so far as to suggest that there ought to be compiled and kept by the authorities, for public information, a list of “principal tenants” with the repts paid by them to the owners and the rents charged by them to sub-tenants. Even so although some of these rents are an outrage on justice and equity, have not the owners the remedy in their own hands by imposing deterrent restrictions on their “principal tenants” in originally letting houses? The views of others of our readers will be welcomed on all aspects of the rents question.

label: text
text: Lengthy evidence was taken before Mr. J. H. B. Nihill at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday when seven members of the crew of the Standard Oil Company's lighter "Delawar" stood charged with larceny of 16 cases of tin plates.

label: text
text: "SOCONY" PROSECUTION.

label: paragraph_title
text:
SEVEN LIGHTER MEN
CONVICTED.

label: text
text: Mr. F. G. Vaux prosecuted on behalf of the Standard Oil Company, while Mr. W. B. Hind appeared for five of the defendants, the other two being unrepresented.

label: text
text: The case against the men was that they stole the cargo which was part of that discharged into the lighter by the s.s. "Speybank," the theft taking place while the lighter was taking shelter from the typhoon in Tsun Wan Bay.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE.

label: text
text: After hearing evidence, His Worship convicted all the defendants, the first being sentenced to nine months' hard labour, the second and third to six months' hard labour, and the others to three months' hard labour.

label: text
text: OWNER REPLIES.

label: text
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mall"]
Sir,—It is all very well for tenants to rush into print to air their imaginary grievances about high rents. As an owner I have kept some of the impertinent letters I received from some of my tenants in the control days, when I was seeking high and low to find accommodation for my brother who had then retired from his position in Kwangsi.

label: text
text:
The principal tenant of one flat, rental $26 per mensem, wanted me to pay him $500 gratuity before he would surrender possession to me, so that my brother could live in my house. Times have now changed and the fortunes of war will fluctuate again.
One argument by tenants is that we bought at the height of the boom and now fleece innocent householders to repair our errors of judgment. This does not enter into the question at all. I was not forced to buy when prices were high. My tenant is not bound to occupy my property. If he thinks the rent prohibitive; led him move out to suburbs and get a flat at $25 a month.

label: text
text: This leads me on to another fruit. Chinese tenants are not ventilating their grouses in print. They have their "face" to preserve. To them, the payment of more rent is better than telling the public that one's landlord has "changed" $184 into $260. I am sure that residents in the more select parts of the Colony would have found "other methods than this" futile, and puerile, attempt to "how up the landlord class." Enclosing my card.

label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong. July 30.

label: text
text: EXORBITANT RENT INCREASES.

label: paragraph_title
text: 一

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir,—I shall be grateful if you will kindly publish the following few home truths in your paper for the benefit of the powers that be. The present high cost of living—largely due to exorbitant rents—is making it almost an impossibility for a Britisher to live in this British Colony.

label: text
text: I may state that I have been a resident of the Colony for the past twenty-five years and have always done my utmost to assist the Government by offering my services during any political or industrial disturbance. I have also served my Country as a soldier and as a volunteer for twenty-two years. I therefore consider that I am justly entitled to some consideration from the Government during this time of stress.

label: text
text: I have just received a notice from my landlord stating that my rent will be increased by sixty Dollars per month as from the 1st August, 1926. When I

label: text
text:
The same the tenant of my present house, eighteen months ago, my monthly rental was $125. Since that time the Government, on behalf of the Landlords, allowed an increase of 15 per cent., which I, of course, had to pay. The landlord knowing that he has a free hand, now the Rents Ordinance has been repealed, has increased my rent by $60. Am I to be turned out of my house, which will certainly happen unless the Government gives that assistance in the way of a Fair Rents Board or other methods of stemming such exorbitant demands.
Landlords are increasing rents and at the same time expect tenants to keep property in good repair. Is it fair?

label: text
text: Yours, etc.

label: paragraph_title
text:
No. 5, Aimai Villas,
Kowloon.

label: paragraph_title
text: A DISGUSTING PRACTICE.

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir,—I shall be grateful if you will kindly afford a little space in your valuable columns to a matter of great importance concerning public health.

label: text
text: I refer to the Kowloon Mortuary which although when built years ago was on an isolated site, is now in the very centre of a residential district and a source of most disagreeable annoyance and even danger to the occupants of adjacent buildings.—To take only one instance: last evening (July 29) at about 9 p.m. a police van drove into Waterloo Road and deposited approximately twenty unnailed coffins by the roadside in front of the mortuary. These contained bodies in a very advanced stage of decay and the smell therefrom was so intolerable that a number of nearby residents assembled at the Yaumati Police Station with a complaint and request for the immediate removal of the bodies. Subsequently the coffins were removed from the roadway and taken inside the mortuary, although the stench continued unabated, and the fact remains that under present conditions the Kowloon mortuary constitutes a very grave public danger.

label: text
text: With so much apparent concern for the health of the people it is very astonishing that the Government can have overlooked a condition so previously inimical to the general welfare.

label: text
text:
Surely it is obvious to all that the Waterloo Road and its vicinity is no longer a desirable or suitable situation for a public morgue, and that same should be removed to some less populous districts.
Having sold or leased ground for the erection of dwelling houses is it not up to the Government to see that these buildings are fit for healthy occupation and not subject to incessant bad smells?—Indeed the public has every right to demand that the Government see that a locality they have sanctioned as a residential district is made safe, sanitary and healthy, by the removal of the mortuary from the midst of dwelling houses.

label: text
text: Thanking you for your courtesy in publishing this.

label: text
text:
Yours faithfully, DISGUSTED.
Honzkong, July 30.

label: paragraph_title
text: HEAVY FALL NEAR TAIKOO DOCK.

label: paragraph_title
text: WORKMEN SCATTER.

label: text
text: A fall of about 2,000 tons of debris yesterday outside the entrance to Taikoo. Dockyard, near Sai Wan Terrace, was fortunately not attended by loss of life, workmen who were leaving at the time having a narrow escape.

label: text
text:
The landslide occurred about mid-day as a large number of the employees were leaving the Dockyard and there would probably have been some casualties if the slide which brought down the bulk of the debris had not been preceded by a smaller one which warned the men and enabled them to scatter in time.

label: text
text: Estate in Hongkong amounting to $16,507 was left by the late Mr. William Stewart Davidson, formerly a well-known resident of Shanghai. Probate of the will in respect of his estate in Hongkong has been granted in the Supreme Court.

label: text
text: Probate has also been granted of the will of the late Mr. Yeung Shut-leung which is somewhat curiously phrased. It opens with the following words:—“A man's life does not exceed a period of several tens of winter and summer and his birth and death will come to pass one day. I am at present continuously ill although still in good health.”

label: text
text: The estate has been valued at over $17,000.

label: paragraph_title
text: Better Value.

label: text
text: A rich lady, accompanied by her maid, had just selected a picture for her drawing-room, representing a group of four peaches and a cut melon.

label: text
text: "How much?" she inquired 02 the dealer.

label: text
text:
"Oh, madame," whispered the maid; "don't buy it. I saw a much finer one at another shop for $28."
"Yes, but how do you know it was better?"

label: text
text: "Why, there was at least 12 peaches, and the melon wasn't cut!"

label: text
text: Local Chinese theatre-goers will be pleased to hear that Mr. Sit Kok-seen, the famous matinee Idol, is back in Hongkong, after a stay of over a year in Shanghai. Mr. Sit has deserted the old-style Cantonese stage, on which he rose from an amateur to a "big star"—in the melodramatic heroic roles—in a year or two. In Shanghai, he felt the magnetism of the cinema world. He is at present the managing director of the Ideal Motion Film Co. and is down in Hongkong for a few days on business. His many friends are trying to induce him to return to his first love and give a few performances here. Mr. Sit (his foreign name is S. C. Harrey) was educated at one of the grant-in-aid schools in Hongkong.
